title: Hevel: Vapor, Breath, Vanity
lead: Hevel is the Hebrew word for a breath or a puff of vapor, something real but brief and impossible to grasp. Ecclesiastes uses it about thirty-eight times as its verdict on life under the sun. Older English Bibles render it "vanity" and many modern ones "meaningless"; this site keeps the image, "vapor."

sections.b: In its plain sense hevel is breath or vapor: a human life is a puff of air (Job 7:16; Psalm 39:5; Psalm 144:4), and treasure gained by a lying tongue is "a puff of breath blown away" (Proverbs 21:6). It is also the name Abel (Hevel), the son whose life was cut short (Genesis 4:2). The prophets use it for idols, which are empty and cannot help: Israel "went after hevel and became hevel" (Jeremiah 2:5; compare Deuteronomy 32:21; 2 Kings 17:15). In Ecclesiastes it becomes the key word, from "Vapor of vapors" (Ecclesiastes 1:2) to the same cry at the end (Ecclesiastes 12:8).
sections.refs: Genesis 4:2; Deuteronomy 32:21; 2 Kings 17:15; Job 7:16; Psalm 39:5; Psalm 144:4; Proverbs 21:6; Jeremiah 2:5; Ecclesiastes 1:2; Ecclesiastes 12:8

sections.b: The Greek Bible chose mataiotes, "emptiness" or "futility," and Jerome's Latin vanitas, "emptiness," which gave English "vanity" (KJV). In modern English "vanity" usually means pride in one's looks, which misleads. Many recent versions use "meaningless" or "futile"; scholars have proposed "absurd" (Fox), "transience" or "fleeting," "enigma" or "mystery," and "breath" or "vapor" (Seow; Miller), and some think the word means different things in different verses. A single image keeps the repetition the writer chose and lets the reader judge, in each place, whether the point is brevity, emptiness or the impossibility of grasping life. In Job, Psalms and Proverbs this site renders the word "a puff of air" or "a puff of breath," as the image suits each verse; in Ecclesiastes, where it is the book's refrain, it is always "vapor."
